title: Intermediate quiz: functions
prompt: Recursion and the register rules behind it: saving `x30` and `x19` in every call, the frames a deep call leaves on the stack, and the frame chain that leads back to `main`.

questions.question: fact calls itself with bl fact. Why must it save x30 before that call?
options: bl will not jump into a function that has not yet returned to its caller
x30 holds the argument n, and the inner call would overwrite it
The inner bl puts a new return address in x30, losing the way back
ret takes its address from the stack, so x30 must be copied there
questions.explanation: bl always writes the address of the next instruction into x30. The recursive bl replaces the address that leads back to fact's own caller, so without a saved copy every ret lands back inside fact. The stp in the prologue keeps the old x30, and the ldp before ret puts it back.
questions.hint: What does every bl write, and where?

questions.question: fact keeps n in x19 so it survives the recursive call. What else must every call of fact do with x19?
options: Save the caller's x19 on entry and restore it before ret
Nothing, since x19 is callee-saved and therefore always safe
Copy x19 into x9 before the call and back again after it
Clear x19 to 0 before ret, so the caller starts afresh
questions.explanation: Callee-saved means the callee does the saving. Each call of fact overwrites x19 with its own n, and its caller (main, or the call of fact one level up) still needs the value it left there. So each call stores the old x19 in its frame on the way in and loads it back on the way out.
questions.hint: Callee-saved is a promise. Who keeps it?

questions.question: main calls fact(4), and fact calls itself until its base case at n = 1. How many frames of fact are on the stack at the deepest point?
questions.explanation: Every call opens its own frame and keeps it until it returns. At the deepest point fact(4), fact(3), fact(2) and fact(1) have all started and none has returned, so four frames of fact sit on the stack, with main's frame above them in memory.
questions.hint: Count the calls that have started but not yet returned.

questions.question: A recursive function has no base case. What happens when it runs?
options: The assembler spots the missing base case and refuses to build it
It runs once, because bl to a running function acts like b
It loops forever without using memory, since each call reuses one frame
Every call adds a frame until the stack is full, then it crashes
questions.explanation: Nothing stops the calls, and each one lowers sp by the size of its frame. Once sp runs past the memory set aside for the stack, the next store faults and the program dies with a segmentation fault.
questions.hint: Each call costs some stack. What runs out first?

questions.question: Which of these is certain to be the same after a bl to a function that follows the calling rules?
options: The flags set by a cmp run just before the bl
The value in x19, a callee-saved register
The value in x9, the first of the temporaries
The value in x16, a scratch register for calls
questions.explanation: x19 to x28 are callee-saved, so a function that uses one puts it back. x9 to x15 are temporaries the callee may overwrite, x16 and x17 may be changed by the code that links the call, and nothing saves the flags.
questions.hint: Only one group of registers comes with a promise from the callee.

questions.question: A helper uses x19 as scratch and never restores it. Its caller kept a running total in x19. What does the caller find in x19 after the call?
options: Whatever the helper last wrote there, so the total is gone
The original total, because bl saves x19 on the stack for it
Zero, because ret clears every callee-saved register first
The original total, since the helper's x19 is its own copy
questions.explanation: There is one x19, shared by every function. The rule that x19 to x28 come back unchanged holds only because each function saves and restores the ones it uses. Neither bl nor ret does it for you. This helper breaks the rule, so the caller's total is lost.
questions.hint: How many copies of x19 does the processor have?

questions.question: Each call of a recursive function opens with stp x29, x30, [sp, -16]! and then mov x29, sp. What does the 8-byte word at [x29] hold in the deepest call?
options: The return address into main, which every frame in the chain shares
The argument n of this call, which bl stores there before it jumps
The stack pointer as it stood when the program first entered main
The caller's frame pointer, the link to the frame one level up
questions.explanation: stp stores x29 at the lower address and x30 8 bytes above it. At that moment x29 still holds the caller's frame pointer, and mov x29, sp then points x29 at the saved pair. So [x29] is the caller's x29 and [x29, 8] is the return address, and following [x29] from frame to frame walks the chain back to main.
questions.hint: Which register does stp write first, and what does it hold at that moment?

questions.question: fact(n) returns n * fact(n - 1). In what order do the multiplications run?
options: fact(n) multiplies first, then calls fact(n - 1) with the product
The deepest call returns first, then each caller multiplies in turn
All of them at once, after the last call returns to main with every n
In the order the calls were made: fact(n) first and fact(1) last
questions.explanation: fact(n) cannot multiply until fact(n - 1) has handed back its answer, so every call waits at its bl. fact(1) returns 1 first, then fact(2) works out 2 * 1 and returns, then fact(3), and so on back up to fact(n).
questions.hint: Can fact(4) multiply before fact(3) has returned?
